name: Furmint

lines.s10: Furmint gives Hungary two wines from one fiery grape: a smoky, sharp dry white and the golden, honeyed sweet Tokaji.
lines.s20: Furmint is the grape of Tokaj, in the volcanic hills of north east Hungary. Dry, it tastes of green apple, quince and smoke, with fierce acidity, and from grapes shrivelled by a mould called noble rot it becomes Tokaji Aszú, sweet with apricot and honey.
lines.s45: Furmint is all fire: a white grape of fierce acidity, at home in Tokaj, in the volcanic hills of north east Hungary. Dry, it tastes of green apple, quince and lime, with a smoky edge and a sharp, mouth watering finish. In the autumn mist a mould called noble rot shrivels the grapes, and those berries are steeped in wine to make sweet Tokaji Aszú. It tastes of apricot, honey and saffron. The dry wine suits pork, river fish or anything with paprika, and Aszú wants blue cheese or foie gras. Tokaj ranked its vineyards more than a century before Bordeaux ranked its châteaux.
lines.sale: Furmint is for the guest who loves dry Riesling or Chablis and wants something new: green apple, smoke and a long, salty finish. Tonight I would set a dry one beside the blackened redfish, and keep a small glass of Aszú for the cheese.

glass.lead: Green apple, quince and lime with a smoky, flinty edge and fierce acidity when dry; apricot, honey and saffron as sweet Tokaji Aszú.

ladder.where: Tokaj's higher, cooler north west arm; the windy hill of Somló
Tokaj's warm south facing slopes; Burgenland; Slovenia's Štajerska

glass.structure: Dry to lusciously sweet. Acidity high and fiery at every sweetness, alcohol medium plus when dry and lower in Aszú, body medium, richer when sweet.

home.home: Tokaj, in the volcanic hills of north east Hungary, where autumn mist off the Bodrog and the Tisza brings noble rot. Dry Furmint is raised in steel or old oak on its lees. For Aszú the shrivelled berries are picked one by one, steeped in must or wine and aged at least eighteen months in oak.
home.abroad: Elsewhere in Hungary it is dry and smoky on the volcanic hill of Somló. Slovenia grows it as Šipon for taut dry whites, Austria's Burgenland keeps a little around Rust, and Slovakia has its own strip of Tokaj.

service.temp: Dry Furmint at 50 to 55 degrees Fahrenheit, 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; sweet Aszú colder, as for Sauternes.
service.glass: A white wine glass for dry Furmint; a small glass and a small pour for Aszú.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary; a young single vineyard dry Furmint can open with a short decant.
service.age: Dry Furmint keeps a decade; Aszú far longer, for decades in a sound cellar.

with.why: smoke and sharp acidity meet the paprika crust
fierce acidity cuts through the fat
the cooking of its own country
sweet against salt, with acidity to finish clean

labels.means: Sweet wine of berries shrivelled by noble rot and steeped in wine; at least 120 grams of sugar a litre.
Once the hods of aszú berries added to a cask; today a sugar band, five or six.
Whole bunches pressed unsorted, as they come: száraz is dry and nutty, édes is sweet.
A named single vineyard of Tokaj; the sites were ranked early in the eighteenth century.
The Slovenian name for Furmint, on taut dry whites from Štajerska.

guest.q: I thought Tokaji was a sweet wine. Is this one dry?
guest.a: Yes. The same grape makes both. Since the 1990s Tokaj's growers have bottled dry Furmint, often from a single vineyard; if the label says Aszú or Szamorodni édes, it is sweet.

guest.q: What does five puttonyos mean on the label?
guest.a: It is a measure of sweetness. Five puttonyos means at least 120 grams of sugar a litre and six at least 150; the word once counted the hods of shrivelled berries added to each cask.

guest.q: Will the sweet one be heavy or cloying?
guest.a: No. Furmint's acidity is so high that even a very sweet Aszú finishes fresh. A small glass is enough, and it sits well beside blue cheese.

guest.q: Is Tokaji the same as Tokay Pinot Gris?
guest.a: No. Alsace once called its Pinot Gris Tokay, and Friuli had a Tocai, but neither had anything to do with Hungary. Both names have been retired, and Tokaji is Furmint from Tokaj.

compare.tell: Dry Riesling is more perfumed, with lime and jasmine and, in age, petrol; Furmint is broader and smokier, with quince and no petrol.
Chenin Blanc shows quince too, but with honey, lanolin and wet wool; Furmint shows smoke and flint in their place, with a fiercer finish.
Assyrtiko is saltier and leaner, with lemon pith and sea salt and little smoke; Furmint is rounder in fruit, with green apple, quince and a smoky edge.

cards.front: Furmint: where is home, and which two styles does it make there?
cards.back: Tokaj, in the volcanic hills of north east Hungary. Dry Furmint, smoky and sharp, with green apple and quince; and sweet Tokaji Aszú, from berries shrivelled by noble rot, with apricot, honey and saffron.

cards.front: Tokaji Aszú: what do five and six puttonyos mean today?
cards.back: Sugar bands, not a count of hods: five means at least 120 grams of sugar a litre, six at least 150. Three and four were abolished with the 2013 vintage.

cards.front: Dry Furmint blind: what parts it from Riesling and from Chenin Blanc?
cards.back: Fierce acidity with smoke and flint and no petrol. Dry Riesling is more perfumed, with lime and jasmine; Chenin Blanc shows lanolin and wet wool where Furmint shows smoke.

questions.q: A blind white is pale lemon and bone dry: green apple, quince and lime, a smoky, flinty edge, a salty finish and fierce acidity, with no petrol and no wet wool. Which grape and origin fit it?
questions.exp: Fierce acidity with smoke and flint, and neither petrol nor wet wool, points to dry Furmint. Riesling would be more perfumed, with petrol in age, and Chenin Blanc would show lanolin.

questions.q: A guest orders a glass of Tokaji Aszú with the cheese and asks how the grapes for it are gathered. What do you tell him?
opts: Shrivelled berries are picked one by one
Whole bunches are cut and dried on straw
Frozen bunches are picked before a winter dawn
Ripe bunches are picked by machine at night
questions.exp: Aszú berries, shrivelled by noble rot, are picked singly over several passes and then steeped in must or wine. Drying whole bunches on straw makes a straw wine, which Aszú is not.

questions.q: A guest wants a bone dry white and points to four Tokaji labels on the list. Which one is the dry wine?
questions.exp: Száraz is Hungarian for dry. Aszú and Eszencia are sweet wines from berries shrivelled by noble rot, and édes means sweet, so a Szamorodni édes is sweet as well.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it: Tokaj, with Somló, Slovenia, Burgenland and Slovak Tokaj as the abroad the Codex's own records name. No New World style of it reaches a list.
The say line follows the Codex's own respelling in the Hungary record, FOOR-mint; the Court's grid holds none for this grape.

No Codex record is contradicted. The profile, the dials and the region records for Tokaj, Somló, Burgenland, Hungary and Eastern Europe supplied the fruit, the smoke, flint and salt, the Aszú notes, the aszú process, the 120 and 150 gram bands and the 2013 reform, Szamorodni, the dűlő, the early eighteenth century ranking, the dry Furmint movement of the 1990s, Šipon and the retired names Tokay and Tocai.

The Codex disagrees with itself on the temperature for Aszú: the Tokaj region record says 10 to 12 degrees Celsius, the service reference 6 to 8 for sweet whites, Tokaji named among them. The entry follows the service reference, as the brief asks, and gives no figure for Aszú beyond colder, as for Sauternes.

A summary of the Hungarian wine body's Tokaj page, read through search, still lists Aszú at three to six puttonyos. The entry follows the Codex's reviewed record (three and four abolished with the 2013 vintage); a checker with the page open should confirm which the page means.
The closing line of the forty-five second description (ranked more than a century before Bordeaux) rests on the Codex's own dates: the early eighteenth century for Tokaj and 1855 for the Médoc.

The parentage (a parent and offspring tie to Gouais Blanc, which makes it a half sibling of Chardonnay and Riesling) stands in Wine Grapes and in general references, but which of the two is the parent is not settled, so it was left out of the entry.
The ladder is a taster's reading built on the Codex's own notes: Somló firmer and more mineral, Tokaj's north west arm cooler and slower, the loess bowls of the south warm.
Skin thickness is disputed between sources read here (thin in the Codex and in most, thick in one), so the entry does not mention it.
Blackened redfish is the one dish from the Creole table, chosen because the Codex's Tokaj record sends dry Furmint to paprika dishes.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.
